progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: C14 (conductivity graphs: hydrochloric acid with sodium hydroxide falls to a minimum, then rises; ethanoic acid rises gently, then more steeply, with a bend at equivalence; hydronium and hydroxide conduct best). C13 (endpoint against equivalence point; an indicator's colour must be seen). C12 (titration, standard solution, pipette, burette, titre, n = cV, the four-step calculation, a titration counts every acid molecule; concordant titres). C03 (net ionic equation for neutralisation; spectator ions). Module 5 C13 (barium sulfate is insoluble). Year 11 (n = m ÷ M, percentage by mass, carbonates react with acid to give carbon dioxide). Not assumed: back titration, excess reagent as a method, conductometric titration as a method, line-intersection reading, dilution correction.
progression.startsWith: Start with an unsuitable direct endpoint or insoluble sample. The video opens: This antacid tablet is mostly calcium carbonate, a base. So why not just titrate it with hydrochloric acid? Try it, and the tablet sits in the flask, fizzing slowly, and the indicator changes colour while solid is still left.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining why a direct titration of an insoluble, slow-reacting solid such as calcium carbonate gives an unreliable endpoint; describing a back titration and why carbon dioxide, when the reaction makes it, is boiled off before the back titre; calculating a mass and percentage by mass from back titration data, subtracting moles and using the mole ratio; explaining when a conductivity titration is useful; reading equivalence where two best-fit lines cross, and saying why dilution bends the lines and how it is kept small; calculating a concentration from the crossing volume. No method choice across pH probes and titrations (chem-m6-c16), no Kjeldahl, no weak/weak conductometric curves, no error-direction tables (chem-m6-g04), no aliquot scale-up (chem-m6-g03).
progression.nextLesson: practice with titration curves, indicators and back titrations (route chem-m6-g04).

teaching.task: A crushed antacid tablet fizzes away slowly in acid, and a dark red vinegar hides any indicator. When a direct titration can't give a clear endpoint, how do back titrations and conductivity titrations still find the amount, and how do you read their results?
teaching.causalExplanation: (1) a calcium carbonate tablet and a dark red vinegar both defeat a direct titration, for different reasons (1); (2) calcium carbonate barely dissolves, so acid reacts only at the solid's surface; the indicator changes before the solid has reacted, then drifts back; dissolved carbon dioxide blurs the endpoint (2); (3) back titration: a measured excess of standard acid reacts completely; the leftover is titrated; the difference is what the sample used (3); (4) boil off the carbon dioxide first, because it would use sodium hydroxide and make the leftover look bigger (4); (5) acid added and acid left over in moles; subtract moles, not volumes, because the concentrations differ (5); (6) the difference, the 1 : 2 ratio, mass and percentage (6); (7) the vinegar would titrate directly if the endpoint could be seen; a conductivity meter does not depend on colour; recall the V and the bend (7); (8) equal portions make equal changes, so two nearly straight stretches; the first points curve and equivalence falls between readings, so read where the best-fit lines cross (8); (9) every portion dilutes the flask and bends the lines; a large volume made up with water (so each portion is a small fraction of it) and a concentrated titrant keep this small, or readings are corrected (9); (10) the crossing volume gives the moles, divided by the vinegar's own volume (10); memory aid (11); two attempts and brief feedback (12 to 15); decision rule and handoff (16); key notes (17).
teaching.conversationalApproach: two samples defeat a direct titration for different reasons: a crushed calcium carbonate antacid tablet fizzes away slowly, so the indicator changes while solid is still left, and a dark red wine vinegar hides any indicator colour. The solid-surface lens shows why the tablet fails; the back titration adds a measured excess of standard acid, lets it react completely and titrates what is left, with the carbon dioxide driven off first because this reaction makes it; the moles bar splits into used and left over, and the worked example subtracts moles, uses the 1 : 2 ratio and finds the mass and percentage. The vinegar goes to a conductivity meter: equal portions give two nearly straight stretches, equivalence is read where the best-fit lines cross, and dilution is kept small. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback, and the decision rule makes boiling conditional on carbon dioxide forming.
teaching.openingDecision: This antacid tablet is mostly calcium carbonate, a base. So why not just titrate it with hydrochloric acid? Try it, and the tablet sits in the flask, fizzing slowly, and the indicator changes colour while solid is still left. A dark red wine vinegar has a different problem: it reacts fast, but the red hides the indicator's colour. So when a direct titration won't work, how do you still find the amount?
teaching.understandingCheck: (A1) "A 0.500 g antacid tablet containing aluminium hydroxide was crushed and added to 40.00 mL of 0.4000 mol/L hydrochloric acid, an excess. After the reaction was complete, the leftover acid required 21.60 mL of 0.2000 mol/L sodium hydroxide. Al(OH)₃(s) + 3HCl(aq) → AlCl₃(aq) + 3H₂O(l). M(Al(OH)₃) = 78.00 g/mol. Calculate the percentage by mass of aluminium hydroxide in the tablet." New base, new ratio (1 : 3), new numbers. Crossed mistake: "no ÷ 3: 182%" (site L18 card 5's ratio error, transferred; the impossible percentage is the check). (A2) "0.100 mol/L sulfuric acid was added from a burette to 50.00 mL of barium hydroxide solution, and the conductivity was measured after each 1.0 mL. The graph shows the results (corrected for the volume added). (a) Explain why the conductivity falls almost to zero. (b) Use the graph to calculate the concentration of the barium hydroxide solution." Ba(OH)₂(aq) + H₂SO₄(aq) → BaSO₄(s) + 2H₂O(l) on the card. Graph: points every 1.0 mL from 0 to 20 mL (author note d), no lines drawn. New system (precipitation removes the cation too), tests reading the crossing. Crossed mistake: "12.0 mL, the lowest point measured" (gives 0.0240 mol/L).
teaching.curriculumScope: Syllabus (NSW Chemistry Stage 6, 2017), as printed: "conduct practical investigations to analyse the concentration of an unknown acid or base by titration" "investigate titration curves and conductivity graphs to analyse data to indicate characteristic reaction profiles, for example:; strong acid/strong base; strong acid/weak base; weak acid/strong base (ACSCH080, ACSCH102)" this video starts from the route's insoluble sample and unsuitable direct endpoint and stops at excess-reagent subtraction and the conductivity intersection. It teaches: why a direct titration of calcium carbonate fails (it barely dissolves, reacts only at the solid's surface, so the indicator changes before the solid has reacted, and dissolved carbon dioxide blurs the endpoint); the back titration (a measured excess of standard acid, complete reaction, boiling off carbon dioxide when the reaction makes it, titrating the leftover acid with standard base); why the carbon dioxide must go (it would use sodium hydroxide, so the leftover acid looks bigger and the carbonate too small); the four-step calculation (acid added, acid left over, acid used by subtraction of moles, the mole ratio), then mass and percentage by mass; the conductometric titration as a method for samples whose colour or cloudiness hides an indicator; why the readings form two nearly straight stretches (each equal portion of titrant makes the same ion change before equivalence, and adds the same excess after it); reading equivalence where the two best-fit lines cross, rather than at one measured point; why dilution by the titrant bends the lines and how it is kept small (a large sample volume made up with water, a concentrated titrant, or readings corrected for the volume added); a concentration from the crossing volume. Not here: why the strong acid conductivity falls to a V and the weak acid rises with a bend (chem-m6-c14 scenes 8 and 9; one callback and a thumbnail only); molar conductivity values on screen (not needed; author note e); choosing among a pH probe, a direct titration, a back titration and a conductivity titration for a range of samples, and what each measurement establishes (chem-m6-c16); the Kjeldahl method and back titrations with excess base (one author note); weak acid with weak base conductometric curves (site Extension; author note f); error direction tables beyond the carbon dioxide step (chem-m6-g04); aliquot scale-up from a volumetric flask and percentage by mass from density (chem-m6-g03); bench technique and risk (chem-m6-p06 and the practical videos).

design.visualSystem: Explainer engine: warm paper stage, handwritten Caveat headings, amber doodle layer. Colour key on screen throughout: hydrochloric acid and "acid added" teal-edged (C12), the titrant sodium hydroxide navy (C12), "used by the sample" amber, "left over" navy; H₃O⁺ teal token, OH⁻ violet, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ small grey spectators, ethanoate grey-violet, Ba²⁺ small pale gold, SO₄²⁻ small slate (C01, C03, C14); conductivity points white dots, best-fit lines pale blue (before equivalence) and violet (after). Board layout (constant, C03, C07, C12 and C14): top-left the short task line; the left column holds the givens card during the worked example (grouped, units attached); the centre holds the lens, the bar, the working or the graph, one stage per line, earlier lines dimming; a plate sits small at the right only when it carries the explanation. Clutter rule: at most three text items bright at once; every label fades when its sentence ends.
